questions.q: A patient with blood group A is mistakenly transfused with group B red cells. Which antibody-mediated reaction is most likely?
options: Recipient anti-B IgM binds donor red-cell B antigen and causes intravascular haemolysis
Recipient anti-A IgG binds donor red-cell A antigen without complement activation
Donor anti-B antibodies destroy the recipient's platelets
Recipient anti-D antibodies cause immediate haemolysis in every first exposure
questions.explain: A group A recipient has naturally occurring anti-B antibodies, predominantly IgM. These bind B antigens on transfused red cells, activate complement and can cause acute intravascular haemolysis. ABO-incompatible transfusion is a medical emergency.

questions.q: An RhD-negative woman has delivered an RhD-positive infant and has no evidence of prior sensitisation. What is the purpose of administering anti-D immunoglobulin postpartum?
options: Prevent maternal sensitisation by clearing fetal RhD-positive red cells before an active immune response develops
Treat fetal anaemia by stimulating erythropoiesis
Destroy maternal anti-D antibodies already formed
Prevent ABO incompatibility in a subsequent pregnancy
questions.explain: Anti-D immunoglobulin binds fetal RhD-positive erythrocytes that enter the maternal circulation, promoting their clearance before the mother mounts an active anti-D immune response. It prevents sensitisation and reduces the risk of haemolytic disease in a future RhD-positive pregnancy.

questions.q: Two parents are both heterozygous for blood group A (Iᴬi). What is the probability that their child will have blood group O?
questions.explain: The possible genotypes are IᴬIᴬ, Iᴬi, Iᴬi and ii; therefore one quarter of offspring are expected to have group O.

questions.q: A patient develops fever, flank pain, hypotension and haemoglobinuria shortly after an incompatible red-cell transfusion. Which mechanism best explains this acute reaction?
options: Recipient antibodies activate complement on donor red cells
Donor T cells attack recipient tissues
questions.explain: Preformed recipient antibodies, especially ABO antibodies, bind incompatible donor erythrocytes and activate complement, causing rapid intravascular haemolysis.

questions.q: Which statement about the ABO blood group system is correct?
options: AB individuals normally have both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
O red cells lack A and B antigens on their surface
A and B antigens are proteins encoded by the HLA locus
Anti-A and anti-B antibodies are always IgG
questions.explain: Group O erythrocytes lack A and B transferase-modified antigens and retain H substance. Naturally occurring anti-A and/or anti-B antibodies are usually predominantly IgM.
